items.title: B200 nested graph breaks | Whiteboard | PyTorch 2.14.1

posts.text: Pro tip: Use PyTorch nested graph breaks RIGHT NOW!!!   On my NVIDIA B200 (provided by my friends @VerdaCloud), I ran a microbenchmark with PyTorch 2.14.1 (CUDA 13.0) and nested_graph_breaks=True. This configuration ran my code 4.53× faster at steady state.
At depth 8, synchronized steady median latency fell from 407.57 µs (without nested graphs) to 89.94 µs with nested graphs. Every pair improved, with speedups from 4.50× to 4.58×!!

The depth-8, seed-0 emitted Inductor code shows 16 wrapper regions × 4 ATen operations without nested graphs, versus 2 regions × 32 operations with nested graphs. Both arms represent the same 64 operations on 1,048,576 FP32 elements.

In retained profiles, each of five untimed invocations showed 16 CUDA Graph replay launches without nested graphs versus 2 with nested graphs. With nested graphs: less fragmentation, larger fused regions, and fewer replay launches.

Cold first call times moved the other way... The sum of the first ten synchronized compiled-call intervals rose from 2.411 s without nested graphs to 3.212 s with nested graphs, a 33.2% increase. The entire net slowdown came from call 1. Calls 2–10 were faster with nested graphs, of course. This is a steady-state win with a disclosed cold-start cost.
The takeaway: inspect emitted compiler fragments and CUDA replay activity, then measure cold first use separately from repeated execution!

USE PyTorch's nested graph breaks!!  RIGHT NOW!!!  One B200 compiler microbenchmark: same 64 operations, 4.53× faster at steady state.

Using my B200s (provided by my friends @[Verda](urn:li:organization:107473669)), I compared PyTorch's nested_graph_breaks=False and True on an NVIDIA B200 using PyTorch 2.14.1 (CUDA 13.0)

In a depth-8 nested-graph-break microbenchmark, synchronized steady median latency fell from 407.57 µs to 89.94 µs. Those are geometric means across four paired seeds. Every primary pair improved by 4.50–4.58×.

The depth-8, seed-0 compiler output shows what changed:

- False: 16 compiled regions, 4 ATen operations each.
- True: 2 compiled regions, 32 ATen operations each.
- Both: the same 64 operations on 1,048,576 FP32 elements.

The recorded CUDA traces also show 16 graph replay launches per invocation with False versus 2 with True. That supports the mechanism: less fragmentation, larger fused regions, and fewer replay launches.

settings.first_comment:
There is a startup tradeoff, however. The sum of the first ten synchronized compiled-call intervals increased from 2.411 s to 3.212 s, about 33.2%. The extra time is confined to call 1, which takes 0.79–0.88 s longer. Calls 2–10 are faster with True. Compiling larger fused programs is the best-supported explanation, but exact compiler-phase timings were not recorded.
 
This is a steady-state win with a disclosed cold-start cost.

The engineering takeaway: compare actual compiler fragments and CUDA replay activity, then evaluate cold first-use latency separately from repeated execution.

Two B200 runs support the same compiler result. We now also have Zymtrace captures from both example workers.

With nested graph-break support, the depth-8 microbenchmark measured a 4.531795× geometric-mean steady-state speedup across four paired seeds. Independent fresh run 022 measured 4.541758×. The runs remain separate.

Neither run qualified startup. In the original run, the first ten compiled-call intervals were 33.2% slower with nested graph-break support, and the startup control also failed.

Nsys shows 16 graph executions without nested graph-break support and 2 with it for one call after warmup. NCU captured one fused Triton kernel per arm: 6.400 µs without support and 20.992 µs with it. With support, each launch does more work. Profiling adds overhead. The published speedup comes from separate unprofiled repeated calls.

Zymtrace 26.10.1 captured both depth-8 workers on B200, PyTorch 2.14.1+cu130 and CUDA 13.0. Both passed correctness checks. The attached CUDA stack views filter by worker PID: 104 exported records without nested graph-break support and 188 with it. Width counts records, not elapsed time. These profiles do not establish an exact CPU/GPU causal percentage.

This is a compiler microbenchmark. It does not establish a training, serving, or cross-GPU gain.

posts.text: @ming85GG Here are the actual Nsight Systems and Nsight Compute captures with and without nested graph-break support on B200 / PyTorch 2.14.1+cu130. The timeline is rendered from Nsys, with exact event spans and a shared scale.

NCU recorded one fused Triton kernel: 6.400 µs without nested graph-break support and 20.992 µs with it. With support, each launch does more work. These kernel durations do not measure the full-call speedup.

With nested graph-break support, Nsys shows 2 graph executions instead of 16. Internal nodes are hidden. Unprofiled repeated calls measured the speedup. Profiling adds overhead. NCU used 9 replay passes. This image shows one call after warmup.

With CUDA Graph replay off, nested graph-break support gave 3.29×/3.27× tail speedups (two seeds, last 1,000 calls), versus 4.55×/4.38× with replay on. GPU spans for profiled calls 3–5 were excluded with support. An exact CPU/GPU causal split is unproven.

posts.text:
The original steady-state gains were 2.87× at depth 4 and 4.53× at depth 8. In a separate 4,000-call depth-8 follow-up, total wall time was ahead from call 1 in seed 0. Seed 1 crossed at call 3,007 and stayed ahead. This includes compilation and between-call time, but excludes imports, input setup, and the eager reference. With CUDA Graph replay off, neither seed broke even within 4,000 calls. These are observed crossovers, not a universal payback point.

This is a synthetic depth-8 compiler microbenchmark with nested Python frames, one explicit graph break, and the same 64 FP32 operations. It is not a training step or a nested-loop benchmark. Backward passes, optimizers, and representative models were not tested, so the 16-to-2 region change does not justify a general default recommendation. A separate B200 test found a steady-state gain with CUDA Graph replay off, but it does not isolate the remaining causal mechanism.
